title: Others' Bad Behavior Can Make Ours Worse, Says Study
paragraphs: A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B has found that individual rule-breaking can quickly turn into widespread misbehavior as people in a group influence each other.
The research included 750 participants from the US.

Working online, participants watched an animated "shooting star" move from left to right across a row of 100 squares that became brighter and darker as the "star" passed. The participants were told to choose the square that lit up the most, which was always somewhere a little to the right of the middle.

However, participants were also told they would get paid more for doing the experiment the further right they saw the brightest square. This incentivized them to "cheat," and choose squares further right than the brightest square they had actually seen.
Furthermore, after each time they saw the "shooting star," they were shown the choice someone else had made for the same animation, and given a chance to change their answer.

Sometimes this other participant had chosen a square near the real answer. Sometimes they'd cheated a little, and had chosen a square a little further right. Sometimes they'd cheated a lot, and had chosen the 100th square.
Participants were also shown this other person's political leanings.
They played this game six times.
In the very first round, before they saw anyone else's results, around one-fifth of participants already chose the 100th square.

But as players saw that others had chosen the 100th square, they began to break the rules more themselves. And they broke the rules most after seeing rule-breaking from someone who shared their political leanings.
Researcher Lucas Molleman said this aligns with previous studies that have found that people are more influenced by those with whom they share political opinions.
He also explained to The Guardian that while many of us believe we make autonomous decisions, we are often very influenced by what others are doing.
